name: Battle of the Little Bighorn
info: On the Little Bighorn River in Montana Territory, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho forces defeated the 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel Custer in June 1876, the most significant action of the Great Sioux War, which the United States still won.

facts.place: Along the Little Bighorn River, which the Lakota call the Greasy Grass, in the Crow Indian Reservation in south-eastern Montana Territory, now Montana, United States
facts.sides: The Lakota (Hunkpapa, Oglala, Minneconjou, Sans Arc, Brule and others), Dakota, Northern Cheyenne and a few Arapaho, led by Sitting Bull (spiritual leader of the Hunkpapa), Crazy Horse, Gall and others, with about 2,000 able-bodied fighters in the camp; against the 7th Cavalry under Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer, with Major Marcus Reno and Captain Frederick Benteen, and Crow and Arikara scouts. Strength figures: 700 men for the regiment, and 31 officers and 566 enlisted men under Custer on 22 June
facts.outcome: Every soldier in the five companies with Custer was killed, and Reno's and Benteen's men were pinned on the bluffs until the Terry column approached on 27 June, when the Native forces withdrew. The United States went on to win the war.

t: The Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho were not an army raised for the occasion: the village gathered to take counsel, and the 'Strongheart Society' of caretakers and providers, not a warrior class, looked after the camp.

Custer's plan seems to have rested on taking non-combatants as hostages and on an estimate of no more than 800 'hostiles' in the area, a figure that left out the thousands who had joined from the reservations.

The Native victory did not save the Lakota's land: within months Congress cut off their rations until they ceded the Black Hills, and in 1980 the United States Supreme Court acknowledged that the Hills were taken without just compensation.
dyk: Of Custer's command the only documented and verified survivor was said to be Captain Keogh's horse, Comanche, yet over 120 people came forward in the next 70 years claiming to be the 'lone survivor'.
ev: The Treaty of Fort Laramie names the area of the Little Bighorn
The valley becomes part of the new Crow Indian Reservation
Sitting Bull has a vision of soldiers falling into his camp during a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek
General Crook's column retreats after the Battle of the Rosebud
Custer divides the 7th Cavalry, Reno attacks the village and is driven to the bluffs, and Custer's five companies are overwhelmed
The fight with Reno and Benteen continues for much of the next day, and General Terry's column approaches on 27 June as the Native forces draw off
Sitting Bull escapes to Canada, Crazy Horse surrenders and the Great Sioux War ends

sections.background:
The battle belongs to the Sioux Wars of 1854 to 1890, fought as settlers pressed onto the Great Plains. The Lakota had been displaced by the United States in and around Fort Laramie, and white encroachment into the Black Hills, which the Lakota consider sacred, added to the pressure. Most battles of the Great Sioux War were fought on land the Lakota had taken from other peoples since 1851. The Little Bighorn valley lay within the Crow Indian Reservation, set up on 7 May 1868, and the Crow, who had a treaty claim there, had not consented to the Lakota presence. In 1873 the Crow chief Blackfoot had called for United States military action. The Crow and the Arikara became allies of the United States.

In late spring 1876 the Lakota and Cheyenne held their Sun Dance, the most important religious event of the year, which some 'agency Indians' who had slipped away from their reservations also attended. Around 5 June, on Rosebud Creek, Sitting Bull reportedly saw soldiers falling into his camp like grasshoppers from the sky. At the same time the army ran a summer campaign to force the Lakota and Cheyenne back to their reservations, using three columns: Gibbon's from Fort Ellis, Crook's from Fort Fetterman and Terry's, which included the 7th Cavalry, from Fort Abraham Lincoln. Crook's column retreated after the Battle of the Rosebud on 17 June, and the army's plans to converge around 26 or 27 June went awry.
sections.forces:
The Native camp held Lakota of several divisions (Hunkpapa, Oglala, Minneconjou, Sans Arc, Brule and others), Dakota, Northern Cheyenne and five Arapaho men who had come close by accident on a hunting trip and were nearly killed by Lakota who took them for scouts until Two Moons intervened. Sitting Bull was the Hunkpapa spiritual leader; Crazy Horse, Gall, Hump, Two Moons and many others are named among the leaders. The tribes had gathered to take counsel and did not form an army or warrior class. About 2,000 able-bodied fighters took part. They carried war clubs, lances and bows, mostly trade muskets, and about 200 Winchester Model 1866 repeating rifles. Captain Weir later saw some 1,800 lodges.

The 7th Cavalry had been formed after the Civil War, and Custer commanded it as lieutenant colonel because Colonel Sturgis was on detached duty. About 20 per cent of the troopers, 139 of 718, had enlisted in the previous seven months. On 22 June Terry sent 31 officers and 566 enlisted men under Custer on a reconnaissance in force. Custer declined Gatling guns and an extra battalion of the 2nd Cavalry. The troopers carried the Springfield Model 1873 carbine and Colt revolver, without sabres, and Crow and Arikara scouts went with them. The army worked from an agents' estimate of no more than 800 'hostiles' in the area, and on 25 June Custer divided the regiment into Reno's three troops, Benteen's three, five under himself and one with the pack train.
sections.course:
On the evening of 24 June Custer's scouts reached the Crow's Nest. Told on the 25th that his trail had been found, and fearing the village would scatter, Custer decided to attack at once. Around 3:10 pm Reno crossed the river and rode towards the village, but the Lakota and Northern Cheyenne were present 'in force and not running away'. Reno dismounted his men in a skirmish line, and after about 20 minutes of long-range firing more than 500 warriors turned his exposed left flank. He led a disorderly retreat through the timber and across the river, and reported that three officers and 29 troopers died in it. His survivors reached the bluffs, where Benteen's and later McDougall's troops joined them.

What happened to Custer's five companies is largely conjecture, since none of the men who went forward with him survived. Native accounts, Crow scouts and archaeology disagree on whether he approached the river at Medicine Tail Coulee. Lakota and Cheyenne accounts say that Crazy Horse led a charge on the cavalrymen. The soldiers' resistance broke up, and most Native casualties were probably suffered on Last Stand Hill. The Lakota said the fight with Custer lasted less than an hour; David Humphreys Miller put it under half an hour. At the bluffs the fighting went on until dark, about 9:00 pm, and for much of the next day.
sections.aftermath:
The army's own dead were 16 officers and 242 troopers killed or dead of wounds, with 1 officer and 51 troopers wounded, 52 per cent casualties. Custer, his brothers Thomas and Boston, his brother-in-law James Calhoun and his nephew Henry Reed were among the dead. Estimates of Native dead run from as few as 36, from Native lists by name, to as many as 300; Red Horse told Colonel Wood in 1877 of 136 dead and 160 wounded. A list of positively known casualties holds 99 names, consolidated to 31 identified warriors. Six women and four children were killed at the start of Reno's charge, among them two wives and three children of Gall.

Within 48 hours the camp broke into smaller groups, since there was not enough game and grass. Terry's column came up on 27 June; the Crow scout White Man Runs Him told the officers that Custer's force had been wiped out. The soldiers buried the dead in shallow graves where they had fallen. Crook and Terry waited seven weeks for reinforcements, and Miles took command in October. In May 1877 Sitting Bull went to Canada and Crazy Horse surrendered at Fort Robinson. Congress attached the 'sell or starve' rider to the 1876 Indian Appropriations Act, cutting off Sioux rations until they ceded the Black Hills.
sections.sources:
No man who rode with Custer's five companies lived to tell of their fight. What is known comes from Lakota, Cheyenne and Crow accounts, from the Arikara and Crow scouts and from the soldiers on Reno Hill. Accounts by Red Horse, Gall, Moving Robe, Iron Hawk and Black Elk survive. In 1908 Edward Curtis walked the field with Crow scouts and then with Two Moons and Cheyenne warriors, and between 1935 and 1955 David Humphreys Miller interviewed the last Lakota survivors. Thomas Bailey Marquis gathered Native stories in the 1930s that were not published until 1976, because their claims were unpopular. In 1879 the Army held a Court of Inquiry at Reno's request.

Archaeology has changed the picture. Shell cases found in the 1920s on Nye-Cartwright Ridge and recent work on Custer Hill have led to new readings of the fight, and some now doubt that there was a 'Last Stand' as popular culture shows it. Historians still dispute Custer's route, whether he tried to cross at Medicine Tail Coulee and where the north end of the village lay. Accounts by Curley and by the trooper Peter Thompson are contested, and historians almost universally discredit Thompson's. Native casualty figures vary widely, and the weight of the weapons, such as the Springfield carbine's extractor, is debated, its part in the defeat being judged negligible on the archaeological evidence.
sections.legacy:
Within weeks Congress added 2,500 men to the Army and enlarged cavalry companies. The Sioux were pressed to cede the Black Hills, which they never accepted as legitimate. The Supreme Court's 1980 decision in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians acknowledged that the United States took the Hills without just compensation, and the Sioux refused the money offered and still insist on their right to the land. The Crow, who mourned in their own way, saw an end to Lakota raids; Plenty Coups recalled that his people could finally sleep without fear.

In the United States Custer became a hero. His widow Elizabeth Bacon Custer lived until 1933 and defended his name in three books, Captain Frederick Whittaker's 1876 book idealised him, and Wild West shows spread the image. After 1934, when Glory Hunter appeared, and her death, historians turned to criticism of his decisions. Reno's conduct was examined at the 1879 inquiry, which found him without fault, and Benteen was blamed by some for not riding to Custer. A national cemetery was created in 1879, the site was named for Custer in 1946, and in 1991 Congress renamed it Little Bighorn Battlefield National Monument. An Indian Memorial by Colleen Cutschall, 'Peace Through Unity', stands near Last Stand Hill, and red granite markers for Native warriors have been added since 1999.

summary: On 25–26 June 1876 Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters defeated the 7th Cavalry on the Little Bighorn, killing Custer and every man in the five companies with him. The United States still won the Great Sioux War, and took the Black Hills.
notes: Counts disagree in the article: the lead says 268 dead and 55 severely wounded; the casualty section gives 16 officers and 242 troopers killed or dead of wounds (258) and 1 officer and 51 troopers wounded (52). I used the casualty-section figures in the aftermath and left the lead's 268 out.

The lead says the 7th Cavalry was 'a force of 700 men'; the Background says 31 officers and 566 enlisted men under Custer on 22 June (the facts box gives both); elsewhere 'roughly 210 men' with Custer and 14 officers and 340 troopers on the bluffs.
The lead says the Lakota were 'inspired by the visions of Sitting Bull'; I used the Sun Dance vision, which the article says 'reportedly' happened.

Native strength is only given as about 2,000 able-bodied fighters (weapons section) and 1,800 lodges (Weir). The article says the tribes 'did not constitute an army or warrior class', which I attribute as the article states it.
The 'Arapaho participation' section says the five Arapaho were there only by accident, against the lead's naming of the Arapaho as one of the combined forces. I gave both.
'Annihilated' appears in the article for Custer's force; I used 'killed'. The count of 'every soldier of the five companies' excepts some Crow scouts and some who left the column before the battle.

Disputed: Custer's route and whether he approached the river at Minneconjou Ford, the duration of his fight, Native casualties (36 to 300), the 'last stand' itself, whether the Gatling guns would have mattered (Hunt and Miles disagree).

Left out as thin or unreliable: the 'Hurrah boys' quotation (no source in the article), the survivor claims in detail, Custer's suicide claims, the troopers' mutilation and Native mallet accounts, the popular-culture list, Benteen's testimony in full. The article's line that Custer's field strategy was 'designed to engage non-combatants' rests on Connell, Godfrey and Gray; I turned this into an attributed 'seems' in the takeaway only.

Garbled in the article: 'Two Moons: Arikara/Cheyenne scout' in the scouts list conflicts with the Cheyenne leader of the same name; left out. Also the 'Black Powder (Sioux Firearms trader)' entry and Ellis's 1890s-style passage using slurs were left out.
'Within 48 hours the camp broke up' and 'the Native forces drew off' on 27 June are as in the article; I did not use 'the Indians' last stand'.
